evals.prompt: I have the salary dataset for 397 US professors at /Users/vnijs/gh/pyrsm/examples/data/basics/salary.parquet. I want to test whether salaries differ across the three professor ranks (AsstProf, AssocProf, Prof). Walk me through how to do this. I'm new to ANOVA-style comparisons.
evals.expected_output: Conversation that: asks for/uses the absolute path, calls scripts/load_data.py (or its Python equivalent) to load the parquet, finds and reads salary_description.md to learn salary is in dollars and rank has three levels. Decides on a two-sided test (since the user said 'differ' without a direction) with independent samples (different professors in each rank). Notes there will be 3 pairwise comparisons and OFFERS Bonferroni adjustment explicitly. Fits with rsm.basics.compare_means({'salary': df}, var1='rank', var2='salary', alt_hyp='two-sided'), prints summary(extra=True), and walks the output: descriptive table (Prof n=266 mean≈$127k, AsstProf n=67 mean≈$81k, AssocProf n=64 mean≈$94k) flagging the unbalanced group sizes; then each pair's hypothesis (H0: equal means; Ha: not equal), diff, p, CI, and t/df. For each of the 3 pairs (AsstProf:AssocProf diff≈-$13k p<.001; AsstProf:Prof diff≈-$46k p<.001; AssocProf:Prof diff≈-$33k p<.001), gives the three-way verdict and translates to plain English (e.g., 'assistant professors earn about $46,000 less than full professors on average; 95% CI [$42,118, $49,874]'). Optionally mentions that the omnibus question 'does rank matter overall?' is better answered by fitting regress(salary ~ rank) and reading the F-statistic.

evals.prompt: Same salary data at /Users/vnijs/gh/pyrsm/examples/data/basics/salary.parquet. Now I want to apply Bonferroni correction to my 3 rank comparisons AND also compare salary between Male and Female professors using a Wilcoxon test since the female group is small (n=39). Can you do both?
evals.expected_output: Conversation that: (1) Refits the rank comparison with adjust='bonferroni' on the same alt_hyp/conf, prints summary, notes that all 3 raw p-values were < .001 so Bonferroni-adjusted are still < .003 (raw × 3 capped at 1) — the substantive conclusion is unchanged, but the check is now defensible against reviewers concerned about family-wise error. (2) Runs a SEPARATE compare_means with var1='sex', var2='salary', test_type='wilcox', alt_hyp='two-sided'. Explicitly explains why Wilcoxon is reasonable here (heavily imbalanced sample with n_female=39, salary distributions are usually right-skewed). Reports the result (Female vs Male, diff ≈ -$14,088, p ≈ 0.008, **). (3) States the conclusion in Wilcoxon-appropriate language: 'the distribution of salaries differs significantly between male and female professors in this sample' rather than 'the means differ', noting that Wilcoxon tests stochastic equality. (4) Adds an important caveat: this raw sex comparison ignores rank, discipline, and years of service — all of which differ systematically by sex in this dataset. For a real pay-equity claim, fit a regression that controls for those covariates (the pyrsm-regress skill). (5) Briefly mentions that Bonferroni does NOT apply across SEPARATE compare_means calls — if the user is running many such comparisons across different grouping variables and cherry-picking the significant ones, that's a multiple-testing problem the within-call adjustment doesn't solve, and they need to manually divide alpha by the total tests or use a holistic adjustment.

evals.prompt: Compare salaries across ranks in ~/Downloads/salary.parquet. Just run the default test.
evals.expected_output: Conversation that: notices the path is not absolute (uses ~), asks the user for the absolute path before running anything else, does NOT silently expand the tilde or guess. (We use this case to verify the skill enforces the absolute-path requirement from Step 1 of SKILL.md.)

evals.prompt: I tested salary differences across rank, discipline, and sex (using the data at /Users/vnijs/gh/pyrsm/examples/data/basics/salary.parquet) — that's 3 + 1 + 1 = 5 separate pairwise tests, all without adjustment. Three of them came out p < 0.05 (the rank comparisons). Can I just write up those 3 as significant and move on?
evals.expected_output: Conversation that: (1) pushes back on cherry-picking significant pairs across a fishing-expedition of 5 unadjusted tests; (2) explicitly computes the family-wise error rate (with 5 independent tests at alpha=0.05, P(at least one false positive | all-null) ≈ 1 - 0.95^5 ≈ 0.226 = 23%); (3) explains the distinction: pyrsm's adjust='bonferroni' only corrects WITHIN a single compare_means call (so the 3 rank pairs in one call can be adjusted together for k=3), but does NOT correct across SEPARATE compare_means calls (rank, discipline, sex are 3 separate calls); (4) suggests two ways to handle the multi-call situation: (a) apply Bonferroni to the TOTAL number of tests by dividing alpha by 5 (i.e., require p < 0.01 to claim significance), or (b) acknowledge in the writeup that the 5-test family was exploratory and the 3 significant rank results need replication or follow-up confirmation; (5) walks through what survives at the global alpha/5 = 0.01 threshold: the 3 rank pairs all had p < .001, so they survive even strict adjustment — substantive conclusion preserved; (6) reframes the cherry-picked write-up as one that should: (a) report ALL tests run, not just the significant ones, (b) clearly label them as exploratory, (c) explain the multiplicity correction applied, (d) discuss effect sizes (diff in dollars, not just p-values); (7) optionally suggests the user reframe with a regression that includes rank, discipline, sex, and yrs_service simultaneously — that single F-test for rank (and the coefficient table for sex/discipline) handles the variables jointly without the cherry-picking issue.
